summaries.summary: PP attachment disambiguation is important in NLP because incorrect attachments cause incorrect parse trees and serious Machine Translation errors, especially for English.
Sentence INLINEFORM0 is "I washed the jeans with pockets."
The correct dependency parse tree for sentence 1 attaches the prepositional phrase with pockets to the noun jeans.
Another possible parse tree for the same sentence is shown in Figure FIGREF2.
A statistical parser often predicts PP-attachment incorrectly, may lead to incorrect parse trees, and another sentence is introduced.
Sentence INLINEFORM0 is "I washed the jeans with soap."
The correct dependency tree for sentence INLINEFORM0 in Figure FIGREF3 attaches the prepositional phrase with soap to the verb washed.
Ambiguity requires semantics, since soap as an aid to washed disambiguates attachment to the verb rather than jeans for correct translation.
The work proposes a Dual Decomposition (DD) based algorithm using parallel Hindi corpora, where Hindi case markers and sentence construction make ambiguity rarer.

The parse tree for sentence (4) in figure FIGREF5 attaches the prepositional phrase saabun se to the verb dhoyee.
The case markers waali and se clarify Hindi pp-atttachment, and parallel Hindi sentences are used to disambiguate English PP attachments before outlining the paper.
Related work includes supervised and unsupervised PP-attachment approaches using Maximum Entropy Model, multilingual aligned data, transformation rules, semantic dictionaries, WSD, and SVMs.
A Dual Decomposition based inference algorithm uses English and Hindi MSTParser models and word alignments to enforce agreement between predicted parse trees.
Agreement means aligned dependency edges or projected paths correspond across English and Hindi parse trees, ignoring edge direction, under DD constraints.
The problem is formulated as below.
The formulation defines English and Hindi sentences, parse trees, model parameters, English edges, projected Hindi paths, and projected path scores.
The score of a projected path is the sum of scores of all edges in the path, with definitions in both directions.
To solve the maximization problem in figure FIGREF7, one tree is assumed given while the other and its projected path score are maximized.
An iterative Coordinate Descent algorithm (Algorithm 1) calls the Project Algorithm until convergence, with trees initialized by trained parser models.
Coordinate Descent Algorithm [1] initializes INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 from MSTParser models and includes break and update steps.
For INLINEFORM0 iterations, the project function maximizes agreement with one fixed parse tree, and convergence occurs when trees no longer change.
The Project algorithm (Algorithm 2) predicts a target-language tree from a source-language parse tree and word alignments.
Project Algorithm (tree T, sen S) initializes INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 = 0 and includes loop steps.
INLINEFORM0 ends a loop, and the algorithm returns INLINEFORM2 if INLINEFORM1, else performs INLINEFORM3 and INLINEFORM4.
Lagrangian multipliers start at zero, and argmax in step 4 predicts the best target tree using parser parameters and projected path scores.
Projected path prediction uses two classifiers in a pipeline: one predicts path length, and the second predicts the path given that length.
Path length prediction uses five binary perceptron classifiers for lengths 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, with words and POS tags as features.
Path prediction uses four structured perceptron classifiers for paths of length 2, 3, 4 and 5, trained on separate annotated data.
Hindi and English MSTParser models used 18708 Hindi Dependency Treebank sentences and 28188 Penn Treebank sentences, while classifiers used 1500 ILCI English-Hindi Tourism parallel corpus sentences.
Testing used 100 parallel sentences with word alignments, manually annotated pp-attachment ambiguity, MSTParser baseline, and iterations 10 to 60 in steps of 10.
The MSTParser model correctly disambiguated 54 PP-attachments, while the algorithm marked 64 correctly, improving baseline accuracy from 54% by 10%.
Experiments on iteration numbers plotted in figure FIGREF11 showed the algorithm performed best at 30 iterations.
Lack of gold standard data led to statistical POS taggers and GIZA++ word alignments, whose errors may cascade and cause underperformance.
The approach achieved 10% over baseline but did not beat MSTParser overall, with future work on larger datasets, other domains, languages, wh-clause attachment, and Machine Translation.
